clue.text: America favours me for fireman I'd be bound

parts.note: to be pro something is to favour it
taken as written
America is the US, with the article: the US

explanation.surface: Someone declares that, with America on their side, they would surely make a fine fireman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'd be bound' sounds like 'I'm sure', but it points at the Titan of Greek myth who brought fire to mankind and was chained to a rock for it, as in the play Prometheus Bound.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titan stole fire from the gods for humans and was punished by being chained, so he is a fire-bringer who was bound.

clue.text: Compact ad.

explanation.definitionFit: A powder compact holds a soft pad for dabbing on powder, and a puff is also a piece of glowing advertising copy.

clue.text: Ditch the hope of Welsh nationalists ?

definitions.text: Ditch the hope of Welsh nationalists ?

parts.words: Ditch the hope of Welsh nationalists
parts.note: the ancient earthwork along the English-Welsh border, a ditch and bank, read as the line nationalists would like to see as a frontier

explanation.surface: A political rallying cry urging people to abandon the dream of Welsh independence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditch' looks like a verb meaning abandon; it is a noun, the earthwork King Offa of Mercia built along the border between England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighth-century earthwork of bank and ditch marks roughly the boundary that a separate Wales would claim.

clue.text: There's always one point that seems weird

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
the Roman numeral I stands for one
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that every story has one moment that feels strange.
explanation.walkthrough: E'ER is the poetic shortening of 'ever'; the apostrophe is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something strange and unsettling, as a synonym pair.

clue.text: Has something under the knee

parts.note: a sock is worn on the leg below the knee

explanation.surface: A remark about someone who keeps a little something tucked beneath the knee.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a churchgoer kneels on a cushion, so it is something under the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A kneeling cushion in a church pew is placed beneath the worshipper's knees.

clue.text: Fun dead ? No, still fast and bright

indicators.note: the 'No' rejects the words as written, telling us to rearrange them into something else

explanation.surface: Someone insists that their fun is not dead at all but still lively and bright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No' signals the anagram: FUN DEAD, rearranged, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Colours that have not lost their brightness are still fast (they do not run) and vivid.

clue.text: Eliot's Theophrastus was of this sort

explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's last book is Impressions of Theophrastus Such, named after its narrator; the plain word means of the kind just mentioned.

clue.text: They wear us out old thing !

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: out signals the letters are put out of their order

parts.note: res is the Latin, the old tongue, for thing

explanation.surface: An exclamation that people wear us out, old thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges US and RES (Latin for thing) to make the answer; people who use things wear them out.
explanation.definitionFit: People who make use of things gradually wear them down.

clue.text: Herrick's maids in the garden

explanation.definitionFit: Robert Herrick's collection of poems bears this title, and in Greek myth the nymphs of that name tended a garden of golden apples.

clue.text: A name for the youngest brother of Wordsworth's little maid ?

definitions.text: A name for the youngest brother of Wordsworth's little maid ?

parts.words: A name for the youngest brother of Wordsworth's little maid
parts.note: Wordsworth's poem We Are Seven has a little girl counting seven children; a seventh child might be given the Latin name meaning seventh

explanation.surface: A literary query about what Wordsworth's little girl called her youngest brother.
explanation.walkthrough: In We Are Seven the little cottage girl insists there are seven of them, so the youngest would be the seventh, Latin septimus.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin name means seventh, traditionally given to a seventh son.

clue.text: The referee if in trouble blows something other than a whistle

definitions.text: blows something other than a whistle

indicators.note: in trouble suggests the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A football referee in a fix blows something besides the usual whistle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges REF and IF. A fife is a small flute, so its player blows something other than a whistle.
explanation.definitionFit: A fife player in a band blows a small flute rather than a whistle.

clue.text: They mollify, more frequently bob about

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the shilling letters stand round the other word

parts.note: a bob is a shilling, written s; here an s stands on each side
oftener is an old comparative of often

explanation.surface: Some people are more often placating others, bobbing about to keep everyone happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bob' is old British slang for a shilling, abbreviated s; 'about' puts the s on both sides of OFTENER.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that soothe or pacify make people gentler and calmer.

clue.text: Eros, as a space wanderer

parts.note: Eros here is not the god of love but the minor planet of that name, a rocky body drifting through space

explanation.surface: The god of love imagined as a drifter in outer space.
explanation.walkthrough: Eros sounds like the Greek god, but it is the name of a minor planet that passes near the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is a minor planet, one of the small rocky bodies orbiting the Sun.

clue.text: Discriminatory smack

definitions.meaning: fine judgement in matters of style, the faculty of discriminating
a flavour or slight trace, as in a smack of garlic

explanation.definitionFit: Good judgement in aesthetic matters is discernment, and a flavour or hint of something is a smack of it.

clue.text: Garrulous ringside commentator ?

parts.note: a talkative boxing commentator, read as one who chatters in a box, the boxing world being the ring

explanation.surface: A broadcaster at a boxing match who never stops talking.
explanation.walkthrough: The commentator chatters and is linked to the boxing ring, so he is a chatter-box.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who talks endlessly is a familiar idiom for someone garrulous.

clue.text: A heap of sleep for a young sheep tender

definitions.text: A heap of sleep for a young sheep tender

parts.words: A heap of sleep for a young sheep tender
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme the boy who looks after the sheep is found under a heap of hay, fast asleep

explanation.surface: A pile where a young shepherd boy takes his nap.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme Little Boy Blue asks where the boy who looks after the sheep is: under the conical pile of hay, fast asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A conical pile of hay in a field is where the rhyme's shepherd boy lies sleeping.

clue.text: Wren's fruit-tree abode in Kensington

parts.note: the garden building at Kensington Palace, credited to Sir Christopher Wren's office, built to house citrus trees

explanation.surface: A small bird's home in a fruit tree in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wren' looks like the bird nesting in a tree; it is the architect Sir Christopher Wren, whose office designed Kensington Palace in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A glasshouse or gallery built to shelter citrus trees through winter, like the one at Kensington Palace.

clue.text: Drive one round the bend, that official " No " !

parts.note: to dement is to drive someone mad, round the bend
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that the official refusal will drive them mad.
explanation.walkthrough: DEMENT is an old verb meaning to drive (round the bend); I is one. A démenti is a French word for an official denial.
explanation.definitionFit: A démenti is a formal government denial of a report, borrowed from French.

clue.text: No hugger-mugger Mrs. Moo's

parts.note: neat means tidy, not hugger-mugger, and neat is also old word for cattle; Mrs Moo, a cow, lives in a cattle shed

explanation.surface: A tidy home for a cow, nothing jumbled about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat means tidy (the opposite of hugger-mugger, muddled) and is also an old word for cattle, so the cow's home is a neat house.
explanation.definitionFit: A shed for cattle, neat being an old word for oxen and cows.

clue.text: Old citizens almost publishable in church

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so one letter is dropped

parts.note: the banns of marriage are read out in church before a wedding

explanation.surface: Elderly residents who are nearly fit to be announced from the pulpit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops an N from THE BANNS, the announcement of a forthcoming marriage made in an English parish church.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of ancient Thebes in Greece were citizens of an old city-state.

clue.text: " Our — travels yet the loved hillside " (Arnold)

definitions.text: " Our — travels yet the loved hillside " (Arnold)

parts.words: Our — travels yet the loved hillside
parts.note: a line from Matthew Arnold's poem about the Oxford wanderer, with the gap to be filled by the word for that wandering student

explanation.surface: A quotation from Matthew Arnold with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Arnold's Thyrsis, which recalls his earlier poem The Scholar-Gipsy about an Oxford student who wandered the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold's wandering Oxford student is a learned person, the figure of The Scholar-Gipsy.

clue.text: Miss Aylmer having dined looks florid

parts.note: Rose Aylmer is the subject of a famous short poem by Walter Savage Landor
having dined is to have eaten, past tense ate

explanation.surface: A young lady who has eaten a good dinner looks flushed.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose Aylmer is the girl mourned in Walter Savage Landor's short poem; 'looks' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a flushed pink complexion, as synonyms.

clue.text: Rests then gets to work again, the model

definitions.text: gets to work again, the model

explanation.definitionFit: To lie at ease is to rest, and an artist's model who poses once more re-poses.

clue.text: Stick in the mud

parts.note: not the idiom for a dull person but a literal verb: to trap in a bog

explanation.surface: A dull, unadventurous person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick in the mud' reads as a noun for a stuffy person; it is a verb, to sink something in a bog.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare verb means to plunge into or entangle in a bog or swamp.

clue.text: Well done Madam !

parts.note: the Italian cheer for a performer, given its feminine ending when it is aimed at a woman

explanation.surface: Applause for a woman's fine achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian cry of applause takes a feminine ending when addressed to a female performer.
explanation.definitionFit: The feminine form of the Italian shout of approval is used to applaud a woman.

clue.text: What they would buy that get shoved in pubs

definitions.text: What they would buy that get shoved in pubs

parts.words: What they would buy that get shoved in pubs
parts.note: the coins pushed along a board in the pub game shove-ha'penny, and what each would buy in a shop

explanation.surface: A question about the purchasing power of drinkers ejected from bars.
explanation.walkthrough: Shove-ha'penny is a British pub game in which old halfpenny coins are pushed up a board; a halfpenny's worth was a ha'p'orth.
explanation.definitionFit: A halfpennyworth is the amount a halfpenny coin would purchase.

clue.text: To sum up, it's not old hat!

explanation.definitionFit: A summary restates the main points, and a tyre with new tread fitted, or anything capped afresh, is renewed rather than old.

clue.text: Films are a sensitive subject for this town

definitions.text: Films are a sensitive subject for this town

parts.words: Films are a sensitive subject for this town
parts.note: the town in northern France shares its name with the glass piece that focuses light onto photographic film

explanation.surface: A town where cinema is a touchy topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sensitive' points at light-sensitive film, which a camera's glass focuses on; the town is Lens in the Pas-de-Calais.
explanation.definitionFit: Lens is a mining town in northern France whose name is also the camera's focusing glass.

clue.text: Long lists of what happens when a necklace breaks

definitions.text: what happens when a necklace breaks

explanation.definitionFit: Lists of names to be prayed for were long rolls, and when a string snaps each bead rolls away.

clue.text: The Veuve's-inexhaustible

parts.note: Veuve is French for widow; the Bible's widow of Zarephath had a jar of oil that never ran out

explanation.surface: A champagne house's supply that never runs dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veuve' suggests the champagne Veuve Clicquot, but it is just French for widow: the widow's small jar in 1 Kings 17 never emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: A small earthenware jar, like the widow's that held oil which never ran out.

clue.text: Kiss the beaming boy ? He sees through us !

parts.note: X is the cross written for a kiss
Ray is a boy's name, and a ray is a beam

explanation.surface: A request to kiss the smiling lad, who can see right through us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaming' looks like smiling, but the boy is Ray, a name that is also a beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiographs show the inside of the body, letting a doctor look through the patient.

clue.text: No amateur's Oriental verses-they don't scan

parts.note: a professional, pro, is no amateur; with the possessive s it gives pro's
E stands for eastern
verses are poems

explanation.surface: A professional's Eastern verses that fail to keep to a metre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scan' means follow a regular metre; poems written in prose have none.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetic pieces written without metre do not follow a regular rhythm.
